title: Your Money Plan
description: The whole course on one page, and a date to read it.
wolfLine: You have the pieces. The page is how you keep them.

lessons.title: The Whole Path
lessons.summary: One page that already has names.

steps.title: You have the pieces
steps.body: Income comes in. A budget gives it jobs. An [[emergency fund]] sits in cash. High-interest debt gets a plan. Insurance covers the catastrophe. A [[three-fund portfolio|three-fund-portfolio]] takes the long money, usually starting with the [[employer match|employer-match]]. A [[will]] and the [[beneficiary]] forms cover the ending. This unit does not add a new trick. It puts the pieces in one place.

steps.prompt: Which pile is cash on purpose?
choices: The stock index fund for age 65
A coin you cannot afford to lose
steps.explain: Cash. The long fund is allowed to fall. The coin is not the plan.

steps.prompt: The match is optional if you prefer to pick a single stock.
steps.explain: The match is pay. A single stock is a bet you already learned to keep small.

steps.prompt: What does the will not replace?
choices: A beneficiary form that still names the wrong person
A list of what you own
steps.explain: The form wins for that account. The will does not edit it.

steps.prompt: The long investment in this course is a cheap, broad ___ portfolio.
steps.explain: Three-fund. Home stocks, the rest of the world, and bonds.

steps.title: Four thousand dollars
steps.body: This drill is a $4,000 month. Needs are at least $2,200. Goals, the emergency fund top-up and the investing transfer together, are at least $800. Wants get whatever is left, and at least $200. Assign every dollar.

steps.prompt: Assign all $4,000. Meet each floor.
steps.explain: The floors are $2,200, $800, and $200, which add to $3,200. The other $800 can sit in wants, so a simple fill ends at $1,000 of wants.

steps.prompt: Needs, goals, and wants: how many dollars are those three floors before the extra?
Wants are allowed to take the rent money if the month looks dull.
steps.explain: Needs have a floor. Wants get what is left after the floors, not before them.

steps.prompt: What is inside the goals floor in this drill?
choices: The cash top-up and the investing transfer
steps.explain: Safety and the long transfer. Not a promise, and not a stranger’s text.

lessons.title: The Yearly Look
lessons.summary: A date you picked, not a red afternoon.

steps.title: Once, on purpose
steps.body: Pick a date. Read the balances, confirm the [[emergency fund]], rebalance if the mix drifted, and update [[beneficiary]] forms if the family changed. Then close the app. A [[recession]] headline is not an extra meeting.

steps.prompt: Put the yearly look in order.
items: Confirm the emergency fund is still funded
Rebalance only if the mix drifted from its target
Update beneficiary forms if the family changed
steps.explain: See the money, protect the cash pile, fix the mix if it drifted, then the names on the forms.

steps.prompt: The yearly look means selling because the screen is red.
steps.explain: Red is not a new date. Rebalance if the mix drifted. Do not invent a new plan from one afternoon.

steps.prompt: When do the beneficiary forms get a look even if the mix is fine?
choices: After a birth, a death, a marriage, or a divorce
After a good week in the market
Never, because the will covers them
steps.explain: Family changes. The will does not rewrite the forms.

steps.prompt: Do this on a date you ___, then close it.
steps.explain: Chose. The date is the discipline.

lessons.title: When Life Changes
lessons.summary: A person changes the papers. A red month does not.

steps.title: Two kinds of news
steps.body: A child, a marriage, a divorce, a death, or a job loss can change the plan. A red month in a fund you need at 65 does not. Job loss spends the [[emergency fund]]. It does not, by itself, rewrite a 30-year mix.

docs.title: A new child
docs.subtitle: The will is out of date

docs.title: A red month
docs.subtitle: The goal is still decades away

steps.prompt: Which page means you update the will?
steps.explain: A child needs a guardian. A $1,500 drop in a long fund is the reason you wrote the “do not sell on a red month” rule.

doc.title: A red month
doc.subtitle: The goal is still decades away

steps.prompt: How many dollars did the long fund fall on the red-month page? Enter the drop as a positive number.
steps.explain: The line is −$1,500, a drop of $1,500. The date you need the money did not move.

steps.prompt: A 15-style red month is a reason to throw out the three-fund mix.
steps.explain: The mix changes when the date changes. A down month is what the mix was built to survive.

steps.prompt: You lose the job. What do you spend first?
choices: The retirement fund dated for age 65
steps.explain: Cash. The retirement date is still out there. Margin is still a skip.

lessons.title: The Page Itself
lessons.summary: Three lines you can actually read.

steps.title: Small enough to reread
steps.body: This page is a finished sketch: $1,000 in the emergency fund, $100 a month invested, and $36,000 a year of spending. Twenty-five times that spending is a $900,000 [[FI number|fi-number]]. You may not have the $900,000. The page is how you remember what the $100 is for.

doc.title: One page
doc.subtitle: The whole course, in three lines
doc.note: The FI sketch on the spending line is 25 times $36,000, which is $900,000. It is a target, not a balance.

steps.prompt: How many dollars are in the emergency fund on this page?
steps.explain: The cash line is $1,000. It stays cash.

steps.prompt: How many dollars a year is the $100 monthly investment?
What is 25 times the $36,000 spending sketch?
steps.explain: 25 × $36,000 = $900,000. A target. Not a balance the market owes you.

steps.prompt: The $900,000 is money this page says you already have.
steps.explain: It is 25 times spending. The page’s actual investing line is $100 a month.

steps.title: Nothing new
steps.body: These questions use the course you already have. [[Inflation]] shrinks a basket. The [[4% rule|four-percent-rule]] is a first-year sketch. [[Medicare]] is at 65. A [[fiduciary]] must put you first. None of these is a product to buy today.

steps.prompt: A $100 basket rises 3%. How many dollars does it cost now?
What is 4% of $500,000, the year-one sketch?
Medicare waits until full retirement age of 67.
steps.explain: Medicare’s window is around 65. Full retirement age for people born in 1960 or later is 67.

steps.prompt: Which promise do you refuse?
choices: A stated fee you can turn into dollars
An offer to look the person up before you hire them
steps.explain: The guarantee. A fee and a lookup are ordinary questions.

lessons.title: Stay Editable
lessons.summary: The page changes when your life does.

steps.title: Not a tattoo
steps.body: The page is right until it is not. A new city, a child, a paid-off debt, or a parent you are caring for can change the spending number, and the spending number changes the target. A noisy week does not. Edit on the yearly date, and edit when the family changes. Then leave it.

steps.prompt: Which event edits the spending number?
choices: You take in a parent and the grocery bill jumps
steps.explain: A real new bill. Two percent today is noise.

steps.prompt: Once the page is written, editing it means you failed.
steps.explain: Editing for a real life change is the plan. Editing for a headline is the failure.

steps.prompt: Spending rises from $36,000 to $42,000. How many dollars did the yearly sketch increase?
steps.explain: $42,000 − $36,000 = $6,000. The FI sketch moves with it: 25 times the new number, not the old one.

steps.prompt: What is 25 times the new $42,000 spending?
steps.explain: 25 × $42,000 = $1,050,000. The target moved because the life moved.

lessons.title: You’re the Alpha Now
lessons.summary: The rank at the end of the path.

story.title: You’re the Alpha now
story.character: You, at the end of the path
story.body:
The rank near the end of this course is **Alpha**.

Cash for a surprise. A cheap broad mix for the long money. Papers someone can find. A date to look again. That is the plan.

steps.title: The last lesson
steps.body:
You started with what income is. You can now read a paycheck, a bill, a fund fee, a beneficiary form, and a retirement sketch. The rank near the end of this course is Alpha. It is not a stock tip and it is not permission to bet the emergency fund.

The plan on the page is enough to continue: cash for a surprise, a cheap broad mix for the long money, papers a person you love can find, and a date to look again.

steps.prompt: Which rank is the one near the end of this course?
steps.explain: Alpha. Pup was the start. A guaranteed return was never a rank.

steps.prompt: Alpha means you should empty the emergency fund into one exciting stock.
steps.explain: The cash pile stays. Alpha is the person who can leave it there.

steps.prompt: What do you do on the date you chose?
choices: Read the page, fix what life changed, and close it
Rebuild the plan from a headline
Send gift cards to a text
steps.explain: Read, edit for a real change, close it. That is the whole habit.

steps.prompt: Put the ongoing plan in order.
items: Keep the emergency fund in cash
Keep the automatic investment in the broad mix
Keep the will and the beneficiary forms findable
Look again on the date you chose
steps.explain: Cash, the mix, the papers, the date. Then go live your life.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Your Money Plan
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: 25 times $24,000 of yearly spending is what FI sketch, in dollars?
A red month in a long-term fund means you rewrite the will.
steps.explain: A new person in the family changes the will. A red month is not that event.

steps.prompt: On the yearly look, selling because the screen is red is what?
choices: Not the point. You rebalance only if the mix drifted
steps.explain: Read, confirm the cash, rebalance if the target drifted, update forms if the family changed.

steps.prompt: $150 a month is how many dollars a year?
